correctness.rationale: The explicit 15-edge Petersen graph has degree 3 at each vertex. A 10-move table checks exact changes 0 -> 1/2 or 2/3 -> 1 at every step, with each target vacant. The block interchanges red/blue site colors; after 20 steps each color class undergoes a length-three permutation on distinct labels. Six blocks (60 moves) restore every labeled agent. The standalone exact-Fraction replay of all 60 moves from the package confirms the premises and state restoration. This proves existence of a strict improving-response cycle and makes no unsupported exhaustive-graph claim.

broader_coverage.reasoning: Neither the one-vacancy potential theorem nor a degree-four regular counterexample implies a cubic counterexample. The variety-seeking two-type theorem has different payoffs: unlike-neighbor fraction may strictly increase 2/3 to 1 while number of different neighbor types stays 1; hence its results cannot subsume this 20/60-move fractional-utility certificate.

originality.rationale: The originating preprint (2023) and later full journal version (2025) explicitly leave the cubic-regular case open while giving one-vacancy termination and degree-four four-vacancy cycles. A full-text comparison found no proof implying the explicit cubic certificate. A later similarly named variety-seeking game counts distinct unlike types and is mathematically nonequivalent; two-type fractions 2/3 -> 1 can improve with its count unchanged. Three targeted semantic-index queries and topical web searches yielded no covering result. Residual unindexed priority uncertainty remains, not a claim of absolute uniqueness.

value.rationale: A directly posed natural boundary question in the source asks if cubic regular networks retain the finite-improvement property beyond one vacancy. A concrete 10-vertex cubic graph, exactly 4 vacancies, only two strategic types and 60 fully reconstructible improvements settles that degree-only conjecture negatively. The result distinguishes a genuine graph-degree obstruction from the source degree-four example; no minimum-size optimality is necessary for its value.
